chunks: "Coils are used because they multiply the magnetic effect of the current.
The field from a single loop is tiny, but if you wind N turns, each turn carries the same current and the fields from all the turns add up in the same direction inside the coil.
So the field is proportional to N times I, ampere-turns, which is what actually creates the force or torque. That lets a small current from a modest supply produce a useful field.
The coil also concentrates the field in the middle, and if you put iron there, the field gets hundreds or thousands of times stronger.
What's special is that the same configuration is an inductor: the inductance goes as N squared, so more turns gives a stronger field but also more stored energy and a slower current rise.
That's why motors and solenoids behave like inductive loads.

There's a design trade-off: for a given amount of copper and a given number of ampere-turns, you can use a lot of thin turns with low current at a higher voltage, or a few thick turns with high current at a lower voltage.
The copper loss is about the same either way, so you pick the winding that matches your supply voltage.
That's why a 12 volts solenoid and a 24 volts solenoid of the same size have different wire."
